title: Water Galura
summary: Water Galura is a North Korea linked threat cluster whose activity is also tracked as GOLD FEATHER, with public reporting describing significant overlap between the two. It is a financially motivated intrusion set rather than a pure espionage group: campaigns have involved broad phishing, credential theft, hands on keyboard access, and in reported cases the deployment of ransomware alongside data theft. Reporting places the cluster behind opportunistic campaigns affecting many sectors and regions, and it has been linked in public reports to a 2024 incident against a payment processing company in the healthcare sector that disrupted billing for a long period. Tradecraft described publicly includes use of legitimate remote access and tunnelling utilities, custom loaders, and operation from infrastructure that is reused across campaigns. Evidence appears in phishing and mail logs, remote access tool artifacts, unusual service accounts, and the overlap of malware families between incidents. Reporting treats the link to North Korean activity and the naming overlap as assessments rather than settled facts.

beginner.definition: Water Galura is a criminal group that steals money and data from companies. Public reports link it to North Korea, and another name for the same activity is GOLD FEATHER. They are known for phishing emails and for taking payments systems offline.
beginner.whyItMatters: Some attackers care about money, not secrets. When they hit a company that handles payments, hospitals and clinics cannot bill and cannot be paid. The effects last for weeks, and patients feel them too, even though no medical device was touched. Understanding this group shows that financial and destructive motives often arrive together.
howItWorks: They send many phishing emails with links or files that look normal.
They steal logins and use them to enter the network quietly.
They use remote access tools and tunnels to keep working unseen.
They look for payment systems and other valuable business data.
They copy data out and sometimes lock systems with ransomware.
They try again later from the same reused infrastructure.
beginner.example: Think of a market where every stall pays a small fee through one office. Thieves do not rob the stalls. They lock the fee office door for three weeks. The market still stands and the goods are fine, but nobody can pay or be paid, and the whole market slowly suffers.
takeaways: Payment and billing systems deserve the strongest access controls.
Phishing is often only the first step, so watch what happens after a stolen login.
Overlapping tracking names mean one incident can appear under two group labels.

objectives: Describe how financially motivated intrusions can disrupt business operations without destroying data.
Explain why payment processing systems are attractive and high impact targets.
Identify evidence of stolen credential use in mail and authentication logs.
Discuss why two vendor tracking names may describe the same underlying activity.
Explain how phishing campaigns scale across sectors and regions.
